module.robtex.checks: Reads the target's public DNS history from Robtex: addresses, mail and name servers already observed, and addresses that are no longer today's.
module.robtex.fix:
For each former address listed, determine whether it is still yours (old server, backup, staging) or whether the provider has reassigned it to a third party, with the "IP RDAP registry" module.
Old server still running and yours: if it is still used, update it and filter it at the firewall; otherwise shut it down, erase its data and cancel the plan at the former hosting provider. A forgotten, unpatched server is a classic way in.
Address reassigned to a third party: check that no current DNS record (`A`, `AAAA`, `MX`, `NS` or `CNAME`, subdomains included) still points to it, and delete it otherwise. An old name server or mail server you no longer control lets someone hijack your domain or your e-mail.
If the site is behind a CDN and a former address still hosts the site, it is probably the origin address, which lets someone bypass the CDN: replace it or restrict it to the CDN ranges (see the "Origin IP behind a CDN" module).
DNS history is public and cannot be erased: do not try to remove it, but make the information useless by taking the former address out of service, changing it or filtering it.
Check what a former address serves for your name with the `curl` command in the snippet below (answer from the old server, refusal or no answer), compare with the current address given by `dig`, then rerun the module.
module.robtex.fix_snippet:
# dig
dig +short example.com A
dig +short example.com AAAA

# curl
curl -sI --resolve example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://example.com/
module.robtex.title: Passive DNS (Robtex)
module.robtex.why: A domain's former addresses reveal old hosting, forgotten servers or the real address of a site that now sits behind a CDN.
robtex.unreadable: Unreadable response from the Robtex service
